title: FCC Authorizes SpaceX to Deploy Up to 1 Million Orbital Data-Center Satellites
excerpt: The Starmind constellation is approved to process AI workloads in orbit, with a first satellite due by November 2033 and full deployment by 2040 — approval, not a launch.
body:
• The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites for data centers in space, approving the "Starmind" constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing, according to Reuters.
  • Authorization is not deployment: under its licence SpaceX must deploy its first operational Starmind satellite by November 2033, 10% of the constellation by November 2035, 50% by November 2038, and the full constellation by 2040, Gizmodo reported.
  • The FCC described this as the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of space-based data centers; SpaceX already has just over 11,000 Starlink satellites in orbit.
  • The agency did not approve every part of the proposal — it declined SpaceX's request on moving higher satellites into graveyard orbits at end of life, saying the company had not provided sufficient information about the disposal process.
Approved, not yet operating: The FCC has authorized the Starmind constellation of up to 1 million orbital data-center satellites. No Starmind satellites have been deployed under this licence. As of November 25, 2026, the announced milestones are a first operational satellite by November 2033 and full deployment by 2040; launch cadence and cost have not been announced by the FCC.

The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday authorized Elon Musk's SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space, Reuters reported. SpaceX earlier this year sought permission to deploy up to 1 million orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth, and the FCC said it was approving the SpaceX "Starmind" constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing.

What Starmind is

SpaceX first formally put the constellation forward in an application submitted to the FCC on January 30, Gizmodo reported. The company describes Starmind as "capturing solar energy in space to power low-cost, high-performance AI compute for Earth." The satellites would function as interconnected data centers, processing information for use back on Earth, linked through high-bandwidth laser communications rather than simply expanding the Starlink broadband network.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfZ5nqGg_xJ/

"This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth."

— Brendan Carr, FCC chairman, in a statement reported by Gizmodo

Carr added, in the statement Gizmodo reported, that by moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment. The FCC authorization also covers radio-frequency links for backup and emergency telemetry, tracking and command across the system, according to reporting on the decision.

The scale, and the conditions

SpaceX is already responsible for one of the largest satellite constellations ever assembled, with just over 11,000 Starlink satellites in orbit, Gizmodo reported. Starmind at full size would increase the total number of satellites in Earth orbit by roughly 50-fold on that account. Other companies, including Google and Blue Origin, are pursuing orbital data centers, and the FCC said it is continuing to review additional proposals.

The licence comes with a long timetable. SpaceX must deploy its first operational Starmind satellite by November 2033, 100,000 satellites — 10% of the constellation — by November 2035, and 50% by November 2038, with until 2040 to deploy the full constellation, Gizmodo reported. The constellation also depends heavily on SpaceX's Starship rocket: deploying hundreds of thousands of satellites would require a launch cadence and payload capacity beyond conventional rockets.

What the FCC did not approve

The FCC did not approve every aspect of the proposal. SpaceX sought a waiver to allow satellites operating above 372 miles (600 kilometres) to be moved into graveyard orbits at the end of their operational lives, rather than being brought down to burn up in the atmosphere; the agency said SpaceX had not provided sufficient information about its proposed disposal process, Gizmodo reported. Scientific and environmental organizations had called for a more comprehensive review: the Secure World Foundation urged regulators to assess cumulative risks to orbital sustainability, and the American Astronomical Society warned the constellation could significantly interfere with ground-based astronomy. The FCC declined to undertake a comprehensive environmental assessment, arguing several concerns fell outside its regulatory jurisdiction, according to Gizmodo.

Before planning on orbital compute

  • This is an authorization, not a service launch — no Starmind capacity is available to buy or use.
  • The first operational satellite is not due until November 2033 under the licence milestones reported.
  • Deployment depends on Starship-class launch capacity that does not yet operate at the required cadence.
